589.title: the rains
589.hook: Rama's monsoon poem: a sky that carried the sea for nine months
589.howItsDone: The monsoon is woven into Hindu poetry, music and festival life; Rama's description in the Kishkindha Kanda is often cited as an early model for the monsoon poems of later Sanskrit and Indian literature.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sugriva crowned, and Rama waiting out the monsoon in the cave on Prasravana.

The smell of wet earth after months of dust. The sky changing color in an afternoon. The whole land seeming to breathe out. Rama, waiting in the cave, describes the monsoon to Lakshmana, and it's some of the most famous nature writing in Sanskrit: a long, beautiful, aching poem. Rama sees all of that, and something else too.
screen: `THE SMELL OF WET EARTH.` → `FAMOUS NATURE WRITING.` → `RAMA SEES SOMETHING ELSE TOO.`

segments.voice: Here's how Valmiki's Rama sees it. The sky, he says, drank the waters of the sea through the sun's rays, carried them for nine months, and now is giving birth to rain: the monsoon as a long pregnancy, finally delivered. He sees clouds piled like mountains and mountains wrapped in clouds. He hears peacocks crying out and sees them dancing. Frogs wake and call after the long dry months. Rivers swell and rush toward the sea. And yet the rain that is lovely for everyone is painful for him. Travelers are heading home, he says. Kings have stopped their campaigns. Everyone is going back to the one they love, and he can't. So every lovely thing he sees, he sees as someone separated from Sita. In Sanskrit poetry that feeling has a name, viraha, love in separation, and Rama in the rains became one of its great examples. Poets for centuries after wrote monsoon verses in the same key: someone far from the one they love, clouds overhead, and the rain saying what they can't. The poem does something for Rama, too, not only for us. Describing the rain carefully slows him down. He isn't raging, and he isn't collapsing. He's looking. Lakshmana listens. And four months, one cloud at a time, begin to pass.
screen: `THE SKY CARRIED THE SEA.` · `PEACOCKS, FROGS, SWOLLEN RIVERS.` · `VIRAHA: LOVE IN SEPARATION.` · `LOOKING SLOWS HIM DOWN.`

segments.voice: Pick one thing in front of you or out the window, and describe it to yourself slowly, the way Rama described the rain: its color, its edges, the light on it, what it reminds you of. Breathe between each detail. If your mind drifts to someone you're missing, let that be part of the looking too, then come back.
The rains. Rama's monsoon poem: a sky carrying the sea for nine months, and every lovely thing seen through missing Sita.

590.title: the rains
590.hook: a new king forgets, a counselor remembers, and autumn arrives
590.howItsDone: Autumn (sharad) opens the Hindu festival season, with Navaratri and Dussehra; in some regions Dussehra celebrates Rama's victory (in others, Durga's), and Ramlila performances are staged in the weeks around it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the rains, and Rama's monsoon poem of viraha, love in separation. Looking slows him down.

Down in Kishkindha, the new king is having a wonderful time, and Valmiki doesn't hide it. Sugriva has his kingdom back after years on the run. He has his wife Ruma back, and Tara is in the palace as his queen as well. He spends the season in comfort, feasting and drinking, with music in the halls. Up on the mountain, the rain falls on a cave. Then the rains end. The sky clears. And Sugriva hasn't noticed.
screen: `A WONDERFUL TIME IN KISHKINDHA.` → `MUSIC IN THE HALLS.` → `THE RAINS END, UNNOTICED.`

segments.voice: Hanuman notices. He goes to Sugriva first, before anyone gets angry, and speaks the way he always does, carefully. You have your kingdom, he says. You have your glory. Now it's time to help your friends. Rama helped you; it's your turn. A king who forgets a friend's service when the time comes loses everyone's respect. Don't wait to be asked. Sugriva hears him, and orders his commanders to gather the monkey armies from every mountain and forest within fifteen days. Friendship sometimes needs a reminder, and the best one comes early and gently, from someone who cares about both sides. Meanwhile the season turns. Autumn arrives, sharad, and Valmiki turns to a new kind of description. Rivers clear and slow down and show their sandbanks. The sky is clean and blue. Cranes fly. Lotuses open. Roads are passable again: the season kings set out. For Rama, autumn is an alarm. Up on Prasravana he looks at the clear sky and knows the waiting time is over, and there's no word from Sugriva. He has been patient for four months. Now he begins to wonder whether his friend has forgotten him entirely. Tomorrow, Rama sends a message, and he sends it by his brother, who is not in a gentle mood.
screen: `HANUMAN REMINDS SUGRIVA.` · `ARMIES ORDERED IN FIFTEEN DAYS.` · `SHARAD: AUTUMN'S CLEAR SKY.` · `RAMA HEARS NO WORD.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who did something for you that you haven't returned yet, not to feel guilty, just to remember. Breathe in and see their face; breathe out and let one small way to repay them come to mind. Then let the plan go and simply breathe, the way a clear autumn sky simply is.
The rains. They end in a clear autumn sky, Hanuman's early reminder, and Rama wondering whether his friend forgot.

591.title: Lakshmana's warning
591.hook: the path Vali took is not closed
591.carry: the path Vali took is not closed
591.howItsDone: Storytellers use Rama's message to Sugriva, the path Vali took is not closed, to talk about keeping one's word to a friend.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the rains ended, and Hanuman reminded Sugriva early and gently: don't wait to be asked.

No messenger. Not yesterday, not today. Rama looks down the mountain toward the city where his friend is enjoying a throne Rama won for him. He doesn't know about Hanuman's reminder or the orders that went out. All he sees is a clear road and a silent city. His patience, which has held through grief and rain, finally gives way. Valmiki lets us hear all of it.
screen: `NO MESSENGER.` → `A SILENT CITY BELOW.` → `PATIENCE GIVES WAY.`

segments.voice: Rama speaks to Lakshmana, first in grief, then in anger. The time we agreed on is here, he says, and Sugriva hasn't come. He's drunk on his good fortune. He thinks I'm weak, a man without a kingdom, someone he can forget. So Rama gives Lakshmana a message to carry, and it isn't subtle. Tell him: the path Vali took is not closed. Keep your word, or follow Vali. It's a hard line. A friendship sworn before fire has weight when it's broken. Rama gave first, at real cost, and he expects faith kept. Notice he doesn't ask for gratitude. He asks for the promise. Then watch Lakshmana. Rama is angry; Lakshmana is angrier. He wants to go down and kill Sugriva today. So Rama, even while sending him, has to calm his brother: don't kill him. Speak gently first. Remind him of the friendship. Usually it's Lakshmana who calms Rama; now the brothers have swapped places. The word that matters here is samaya, an agreement, and also an appointed time. In Sanskrit it can mean both. Rama's complaint isn't that Sugriva enjoyed himself after years of exile. It's that he let the agreed time slip by. A promise has a when as well as a what. Lakshmana picks up his bow and walks down the mountain toward Kishkindha.
screen: `RAMA'S GRIEF TURNS TO ANGER.` · `THE PATH VALI TOOK IS NOT CLOSED.` · `SPEAK GENTLY FIRST.` · `SAMAYA: AGREEMENT AND TIME.`

segments.voice: Think of one promise with a date on it: a visit, a deadline, a reply you said you'd send. Breathe in and feel where it sits in time, near or far; breathe out and let your body relax around it. You don't have to act on it now; just know when it is.
Lakshmana's warning. Rama's message: the path Vali took is not closed. Keep the agreed time.
Your line: the path Vali took is not closed. Even Rama's patience has an end. Until tomorrow.

592.title: Lakshmana's warning
592.hook: a bowstring that shakes a city, and the one person who can calm it
592.howItsDone: Storytellers point to Tara here as a model of wise speech; she is remembered for her counsel as much as for her story.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Rama's hard message went down the mountain with Lakshmana: the path Vali took is not closed.
screen: `THE PATH VALI TOOK IS NOT CLOSED.`

segments.voice: The monkeys at the gates of Kishkindha see Lakshmana coming and panic. He looks, Valmiki says, like the fire at the end of the world. They scramble up walls and into trees. Some grab boulders and branches, as if that would help. Young Angada goes to meet him and is sent running back inside with the message. Lakshmana walks straight through the city, past the fine houses and gardens, and at the palace he twangs his bowstring so loudly that the whole city shakes.
screen: `PANIC AT THE GATES.` → `LIKE THE FIRE AT THE END OF THE WORLD.` → `A BOWSTRING SHAKES THE CITY.`

segments.voice: Inside, Sugriva hears the bowstring, and the party is over. He's frightened, and at first he can't think what he's done wrong; Hanuman has to tell him he let the time slip. He doesn't go out to meet Lakshmana himself. He sends Tara. Of everyone in the palace, she's the one who can calm this. Not long ago she was a widow grieving before Rama. Now she walks out to meet his furious brother, and she speaks with complete poise. Why are you angry, prince? she asks. Sugriva has been careless, yes. After years of hardship he's been lost in pleasure. Even great sages have been carried away by desire, she says, and she names Vishvamitra, who once spent years with the celestial dancer Ghritachi and thought it was a single day. Then she tells him the part he hasn't heard. Sugriva hasn't actually forgotten. Orders have already gone out. Armies are already on their way, from mountains and forests everywhere. Come in, she says. Talk to him. Lakshmana came in furious. He listens, and his anger cools. He doesn't stop being firm, but now he's willing to talk. It's a quiet turn in the Kishkindha Kanda: the person who cools Rama's warning is the same person whose own warning Vali ignored. Tara has been right twice now. This time somebody listens.
screen: `SUGRIVA SENDS TARA.` · `EVEN SAGES ARE CARRIED AWAY.` · `THE ARMIES ARE ALREADY COMING.` · `THIS TIME SOMEBODY LISTENS.`

593.title: Lakshmana's warning
593.hook: an apology, a flood of armies, and an embrace
593.carry: I may have slipped, who doesn't
593.howItsDone: Kshama, forgiveness or forbearance, is listed among the virtues in Hindu texts such as the Bhagavad Gita (16.3), and the reconciliation of Rama and Sugriva is told as an example of friendship repaired.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Tara met Lakshmana's anger with calm and honesty, and this time somebody listened.

Lakshmana walks into the inner palace. It's beautiful, full of gardens, music and fine things, and Valmiki describes it in detail, maybe so we'll feel how far Sugriva has drifted from a cave on a mountain. Sugriva is on his throne, in fine clothes and garlands, his queens around him. He sees Lakshmana and gets to his feet. Now the king of the monkeys has to face the brother of the man who made him king.
screen: `THE INNER PALACE.` → `SUGRIVA ON HIS THRONE.` → `HE GETS TO HIS FEET.`

segments.voice: Lakshmana speaks hard words. A king who takes help and doesn't keep his promise is ungrateful, he says, and for ingratitude there's no atonement. He repeats Rama's message. Sugriva doesn't argue. Everything I have, he says, I owe to Rama. I may have slipped. Who doesn't? But I'm his friend and his servant, and I'll follow him with my whole army. If I've failed through carelessness or overconfidence, forgive me. A good apology owns the fault, doesn't drown in it, and moves to action. Sugriva does all three, and Lakshmana softens at once. You've spoken well, he says. Come and see Rama. Sugriva rides out with Lakshmana to Rama, gets down, and bows with joined palms. Rama receives him with an embrace and asks him to sit beside him. And while they talk, the armies arrive. Valmiki turns it into a parade: monkeys and bears pour in past counting, from mountains and seashores, from forests and snowy peaks, until they seem to cover the earth. The Sanskrit word for forgiveness, kshama, also means patience, and it's also a name for the earth, the one who bears everything. Rama doesn't hold the lost weeks against him. The friendship is back where it was, and stronger, because now it has been tested and repaired. And Rama turns to the real question: where do we look first?
screen: `NO ATONEMENT FOR INGRATITUDE.` · `SUGRIVA: FORGIVE ME.` · `AN EMBRACE, AND ARMIES.` · `KSHAMA: FORGIVENESS, THE EARTH.`

594.title: the search parties
594.hook: four armies, four directions, and a map learned by running
594.howItsDone: Sugriva's descriptions of the four directions are studied as an early Indian picture of the world; many places named in them, from the Ganga to the southern sea, are still pilgrimage sites linked to the Ramayana.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sugriva's apology, I may have slipped, who doesn't, and kshama: forgiveness, a name for the earth.

The rains are over and the roads are open. Sugriva stands before an army gathered from every forest and mountain he rules, and he has almost nothing to hand it: a bundle of jewels, a name, and one direction. The chariot flew south. That's all anyone knows. Somewhere beyond the forests and rivers and seas is one woman, and no one has an address. Sugriva's answer is to split the army four ways, and to give each leader directions so detailed they fill whole chapters.
screen: `ONE WOMAN, SOMEWHERE.` → `A HUGE ARMY, NO ADDRESS.` → `SPLIT FOUR WAYS.`

segments.voice: Sugriva sends Vinata to the east, Sushena to the west, Shatabali to the north, and to the south, where Ravana flew, he sends his best: Angada, with Hanuman, the old bear Jambavan, and others. For each direction he names rivers, mountains, kingdoms and peoples, seas and islands, and strange places at the edge of the world. Scholars sometimes call these chapters the epic's geography: a picture of the world as the poem imagined it. Some names match real places, like the Ganga, the Yamuna and the Godavari. Others belong to myth, like the mountains where the sun rises and sets. How does Sugriva know all this? Rama asks him later. Sugriva answers that when Vali was chasing him, he fled everywhere, and saw the whole world while running for his life. His exile became his map. The worst years of his life turn out to be exactly what his friend needs. And there's a deadline. One month, Sugriva says. Come back within a month, with news, or answer to me with your lives. It's harsh. But it shows how seriously he now takes the promise he once let slip. The armies set out in four directions, and the city goes quiet behind them. Rama, Lakshmana and Sugriva stay behind, which may be the hardest job of all: waiting a month for news.
screen: `EAST, WEST, NORTH, AND SOUTH.` · `THE EPIC'S GEOGRAPHY.` · `A MAP LEARNED BY RUNNING.` · `ONE MONTH.`

segments.voice: Feel the four directions around you: in front, behind, left and right. Breathe into each in turn, then sit in the middle of all four, centered and still. For these two minutes, there's nowhere to go.

595.title: the search parties
595.hook: a ring with Rama's name, and three parties come home empty-handed
595.howItsDone: In paintings and temple carvings, Hanuman is often shown kneeling before Sita and holding out Rama's ring, the moment this token was given for.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the search parties set out, four directions, a map learned by running, and one month. Today the week closes.

Before the southern party leaves, Rama calls Hanuman aside. Of all the leaders and all the armies, it's Hanuman he picks out. Sugriva's confidence in him is obvious, and Rama has his own reasons, going back to that first conversation on Rishyamuka, the sentence with not one word wrong. He takes something small off his finger and holds it out. It's the kind of thing you'd give someone only if you were sure of them.
screen: `RAMA CALLS HANUMAN ASIDE.` → `SOMETHING SMALL, HELD OUT.`

segments.voice: It's a ring, engraved with Rama's name. Take this, Rama tells him, so that when you find her, she'll know you come from me, and won't be afraid. Hanuman will meet Sita as a stranger, a monkey in an enemy city. Words alone might not be believed. A ring she knows will be. Rama is planning ahead for the moment when trust will matter most. And why Hanuman? Valmiki gives the reason: Sugriva is surest of him, and Rama sees his resolve and believes this one will succeed. Hanuman takes the ring, raises it to his head with joined palms, and bows at Rama's feet before he sets out. Then the month passes. The parties to the east, the west and the north search everything Sugriva described: mountains, forests, caves, rivers, cities. They come back on time, and they come back with nothing. No sign of Sita. Now everyone is waiting on the south. The week, from the top. The monsoon poem, the sky giving birth to rain. Hanuman's early reminder, and a clear autumn sky. Rama's message: the path Vali took is not closed. Lakshmana's bowstring, and Tara's calm. Sugriva's apology, and armies covering the earth. Four directions and a map learned by running. And today, a ring, and three empty-handed returns.
screen: `A RING WITH RAMA'S NAME.` · `WHY HANUMAN.` · `THREE PARTIES RETURN EMPTY.` · `THE WEEK, FROM THE TOP.` · then, large: `EVERYONE WAITS ON THE SOUTH.`

segments.voice: If you're wearing a ring or something small you value, rest your attention on it; if not, picture something small that someone once gave you. Breathe in and remember who gave it; breathe out and feel what it carries: their trust, their memory, their hope.
Anguliya, a finger-ring: the one Rama gives Hanuman today, engraved with his name, so Sita will know he sent him.
Your line: everyone waits on the south. One small ring carries a lot of hope. Day five hundred ninety-five, done.

chat.says: Why did Rama give Hanuman his ring before the search began?
options: So Sita would know he truly came from Rama, and not be afraid of a stranger.
To pay Hanuman ahead of time for leading the southern search party.
So Hanuman could trade it for a ship to carry him across to Lanka.
